items.name: Standard form and orders of magnitude

bullets.text: Do arithmetic with numbers in standard form a × 10^k, taking 1 ≤ a < 10 and k any integer.
Write standard form properly (5.2 × 10^30), never in calculator notation such as 5.2E30.
Recognise an arithmetic sequence and find its nth term from the first term and common difference.
Find the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence.
Write and evaluate arithmetic sums in sigma notation.
Apply arithmetic sequences to contexts such as simple interest, using technology (spreadsheet or GDC) to list terms and identify first term and difference.
Judge and predict from real data that is only roughly arithmetic, approximating the common difference.

booklet.label: nth term of an arithmetic sequence

bullets.text: Recognise a geometric sequence and find its nth term from the first term and common ratio.
Find the sum of the first n terms of a geometric sequence.
Write and evaluate geometric sums in sigma notation.
Apply geometric sequences to contexts such as disease spread, salary change and population growth, using technology and identifying first term and ratio.
Link geometric sequences to exponential models (topic 2) and regression (topic 4).

booklet.label: nth term of a geometric sequence
Sum of a finite geometric sequence

bullets.text: Model compound interest with geometric sequences, compounding yearly, half-yearly, quarterly or monthly.
Model annual depreciation with geometric sequences.
Use technology, including built-in financial packages, for these problems; simple interest can lead in to compound interest.
Find the real value of an investment given an interest rate and an inflation rate.
Deriving the compound-interest formula is not examined.
Apply the laws of exponents to integer exponents (products, quotients, powers, negative exponents), e.g. 6^4 ÷ 6^3 = 6 and 2x^−3 = 2/x^3.
Know that a^x = b means log_a b = x (with b > 0), and that log_e x is ln x; introduce base-10 and base-e logarithms.
Evaluate logarithms numerically with technology.
Prove simple statements deductively with numbers and with algebra.
Lay out an LHS-to-RHS proof, starting from one side and transforming it step by step into the other (either direction).
Use the symbols for equality (=) and identity (≡) correctly, e.g. (x − 3)^2 + 5 ≡ x^2 − 6x + 14.
Show how a result can be checked, including checking your own working.
Apply the laws of exponents to rational exponents, with a^(1/m) the mth root (positive root when m is even), e.g. 16^(3/4) = 8.
Use the laws of logarithms: log of a product, a quotient and a power, for a, x, y > 0.
Know y = a^x ⇔ x = log_a y, log_a a = 1 and log_a 1 = 0, and combine logs in examples such as log 24 = log 8 + log 3.
Change the base of a logarithm: log_a x = log_b x / log_b a, for a, b, x > 0.
Solve exponential equations, including by taking logarithms, e.g. (1/3)^x = 9^(x+1) and 2^(x−1) = 10.
Find the sum to infinity of a convergent geometric sequence.
Use the condition |r| < 1 with modulus notation.
Expand (a + b)^n for n ∈ ℕ using the binomial theorem; ℕ includes 0 in IB notation.
Use Pascal's triangle and nCr to get binomial coefficients.
Find nCr both with the formula and with technology, e.g. finding r when 6Cr = 20 from a table of values.
Counting principles may be used to build up the theorem.
Use counting principles, including permutations and combinations.
Permutations with identical objects and circular arrangements are not required.
Expand (a + b)^n when n is rational, so fractional and negative powers are allowed; factor a out of the bracket, leaving a^n outside: a^n(1 + b/a)^n.
Proving the binomial theorem is not required.
Split a rational expression into partial fractions, e.g. (2x + 1)/(x^2 + x − 2) ≡ 1/(x − 1) + 1/(x + 2).
Limit: at most two distinct linear factors in the denominator, with numerator degree below denominator degree.

items.name: Complex numbers and the Argand diagram

bullets.text: Know the number i with i^2 = −1, and write complex numbers in Cartesian form z = a + bi.
For a complex number, identify its conjugate and its modulus and argument, as well as real and imaginary parts.
Plot complex numbers on the complex plane (Argand diagram).

booklet.label: Cartesian form of a complex number

bullets.text: Write a complex number in modulus-argument (polar) form r(cosθ + i sinθ) = r cisθ.
Write a complex number in Euler form re^(iθ).
Add, multiply and divide complex numbers in Cartesian, polar or Euler form and interpret these geometrically.
Convert between Cartesian, polar and Euler forms.

items.name: Complex roots and De Moivre’s theorem

bullets.text: Use the fact that non-real roots of polynomials with real coefficients come in conjugate pairs.
Apply De Moivre's theorem, including the proof by induction for positive integer n and its extension to rational exponents.
Find powers and roots of complex numbers.

booklet.label: Sum and product of polynomial roots

items.name: Proof methods: induction, contradiction and counterexample

bullets.text: Prove statements by mathematical induction (e.g. in complex numbers, differentiation, sums of sequences, divisibility).
Prove statements by contradiction, e.g. irrationality of √3 or of the cube root of 5, infinitely many primes.
Disprove a statement with a counterexample, e.g. n^2 + 41n + 41 not always prime.
Explain why the example is a counterexample; stating it alone is not enough.
Solve systems of up to three linear equations in three unknowns, with a unique solution, infinitely many solutions or none.
Use both algebraic methods and technology (e.g. row reduction, matrices).
Recognise a system with no solution as inconsistent.
Give the general solution when there are infinitely many solutions.
Write and convert between gradient-intercept, general and point-gradient forms of a line.
Find the gradient and intercepts of a line.
Use m1 = m2 for parallel lines and m1 × m2 = −1 for perpendicular lines.
Calculate gradients in real settings such as roads and bridges.
Explain function, domain, range and graph, and use notation such as f(x), v(t), C(n); e.g. f(x) = √(2 − x) has domain x ≤ 2 and range f(x) ≥ 0.
Treat a function as a mathematical model; a graph helps to see the range.
Understand an inverse as undoing the function, as a reflection in y = x, written f^−1(x).
Solve f(x) = 10 as finding f^−1(10); inverses exist for one-to-one functions, and the domain of f^−1 is the range of f.
Know the graph of y = f(x) from its equation.
Sketch a graph from given information or a context, including moving a graph from screen to paper.
Use technology to graph functions, including sums and differences of functions.
Distinguish draw from sketch, and label axes and key features; graphs may include functions not named in topic 2.
Read key features off graphs with technology: extremes, intercepts, symmetry, vertex, zeros, and vertical or horizontal asymptotes.
Find intersection points of two curves or lines with technology.
Form and evaluate composite functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).
Know the identity function, and that (f ∘ f^−1)(x) = (f^−1 ∘ f)(x) = x.
Find the inverse f^−1(x); inverses exist for one-to-one functions, and the graph is a reflection in y = x.
Use f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c: its graph, y-intercept (0, c) and axis of symmetry.
Use factored form a(x − p)(x − q) to read off x-intercepts (p, 0) and (q, 0).
Use vertex form a(x − h)^2 + k to read off the vertex (h, k).
Change from one form to another.

booklet.label: Axis of symmetry of a quadratic

bullets.text: Solve quadratic equations and inequalities by factorising, completing the square or the quadratic formula; solutions are roots or zeros.
Use the discriminant Δ = b^2 − 4ac to decide how many real roots there are: two different, one repeated, or none.
Find parameter values giving a stated root type, e.g. for 3kx^2 + 2x + k = 0.
Know the reciprocal function f(x) = 1/x (x ≠ 0): its graph and that it is self-inverse.
Work with rational functions (ax + b)/(cx + d) and sketch their graphs with asymptotes and axis intercepts.
Find the asymptotes: vertical x = −d/c, horizontal y = a/c.
Know exponential functions a^x (a > 0) and e^x, and their graphs.
Know logarithmic functions log_a x (x > 0) and ln x, and their graphs.
Use a^x = e^(x ln a) and log_a a^x = x = a^(log_a x) for a, x > 0, a ≠ 1.
Recognise exponential and logarithmic functions as inverses; link to compound interest and depreciation (1.4).
Solve equations graphically and analytically, e.g. e^(2x) − 5e^x + 4 = 0.
Use technology for equations with no suitable analytic method, e.g. e^x = sin x, x^4 + 5x − 6 = 0.
Apply graphing and equation solving to real-life situations, including exponential growth.
Apply translations y = f(x) + b and y = f(x − a).
Apply reflections in both axes: y = −f(x) and y = f(−x).
Apply a vertical stretch y = p f(x) and a horizontal stretch y = f(qx) with scale factor 1/q.
Combine transformations; order matters, e.g. sketching 3x^2 + 2 from y = x^2.
Transformations of the form f(ax + b) are not required at SL.
Work with polynomial functions: graphs, equations, zeros, roots and factors.
Use the factor theorem and the remainder theorem.
Use the sum −a_{n−1}/a_n and product (−1)^n a_0/a_n of the roots of a_n x^n + … + a_0 = 0.

booklet.label: Sum and product of polynomial roots

bullets.text: Work with rational functions (ax + b)/(cx^2 + dx + e) and (ax^2 + bx + c)/(dx + e); the reciprocal function is a special case.
Sketch graphs showing every asymptote (horizontal, vertical, oblique) and axis intercepts; link to SL 2.8.
Recognise even functions f(−x) = f(x) and odd functions f(−x) = −f(x); this includes periodic functions.
Find the inverse f^−1(x), including restricting the domain.
Recognise self-inverse functions.
Solve g(x) ≥ f(x) graphically and analytically.
Solve with a graph or algebra when the polynomials are simple (degree 3 at most); technology may be used for these and for any other functions.
Sketch y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|), y = 1/f(x), y = f(ax + b) and y = [f(x)]^2 from the graph of f.
Solve modulus equations and inequalities, e.g. |3x arccos(x)| > 1.
Dynamic graphing packages can help investigate these transformations.
Find the distance between two points in 3D and their midpoint.
Find volume and surface area of right pyramids, right cones, spheres, hemispheres and combinations of these solids.
Measure the angle where two lines meet, or the angle a line makes with a plane.
At SL, only right-angled trigonometry is set in 3D; identify right-angled triangles inside solids to find lengths and angles.

booklet.label: Curved surface area of a cone

bullets.text: Use sine, cosine and tangent to find sides and angles of right-angled triangles.
Use the sine rule a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC.
Use the cosine rule c^2 = a^2 + b^2 − 2ab cosC and cosC = (a^2 + b^2 − c^2)/(2ab).
Find a triangle's area as ½ab sinC.
Draw well-labelled diagrams; use inverse functions for angles (SL 2.2); the ambiguous case of the sine rule is not included here.
Solve applied problems with right-angled and non-right-angled trigonometry plus Pythagoras's theorem; contexts may involve bearings.
Use angles of elevation and depression.
Draw labelled diagrams from a written description.

items.name: Radians, arc length and sector area

bullets.text: Measure angles in radians, as exact multiples of π or as decimals.
Find arc length and sector area.
Define cosθ and sinθ using the unit circle, including angles in different quadrants (e.g. cosx = cos(−x), tan(3π − x) = −tanx, sin(π + x) = −sinx).
Define tanθ as sinθ/cosθ; the line y = x tanθ passes through the origin at angle θ to the positive x-axis.
Know exact trig values for 0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 and their multiples, e.g. sin(π/3) = √3/2, cos(3π/4) = −1/√2, tan210° = √3/3.
Extend the sine rule to the ambiguous case.

booklet.label: tan in terms of sin and cos

bullets.text: Use the Pythagorean identity cos^2θ + sin^2θ = 1.
Use the double angle identities for sine and cosine; diagrams or dynamic graphing can illustrate them.
Relate trig ratios to each other, e.g. find tanθ from sinθ, or sin2x from cosx = 3/4 for acute x, without finding the angle.
Know the graphs of sinx, cosx and tanx, their amplitude and periodicity; domains may be in degrees or radians.
Work with f(x) = a sin(b(x + c)) + d, e.g. tan(x − π/4) and 2cos(3(x − 4)) + 1.
Describe transformations of trig graphs, e.g. getting y = 3sin2x from y = sinx by stretches of factor 3 (vertical) and 1/2 (horizontal).
Model real-life periodic situations (tides, Ferris wheel); note regression technology may not return the form a sin(b(x + c)) + d.
Solve trig equations in a finite interval, graphically and analytically, e.g. 2sinx = 1 on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π.
Solve trig equations that reduce to quadratics in sinx, cosx or tanx, e.g. 2sin^2 x + 5cosx + 1 = 0 and 2sinx = cos2x.
The general solution of trig equations is not required.

booklet.label: tan in terms of sin and cos

bullets.text: Define the reciprocal ratios secθ, cosecθ and cotθ.
Use the identities 1 + tan^2θ = sec^2θ and 1 + cot^2θ = cosec^2θ.
Know arcsin, arccos and arctan: their domains, ranges and graphs.

booklet.label: Pythagorean identity with tan and sec
Pythagorean identity with cot and cosec

bullets.text: Use the compound angle identities.
Use the double angle identity for tan.
Derive the double angle identities from the compound angle identities.
Use relationships and graph symmetry between trig functions, e.g. sin(π − θ) = sinθ, cos(π − θ) = −cosθ, tan(π − θ) = −tanθ.
Understand vectors, position vectors and displacement vectors, drawn as directed line segments.
Use base vectors i, j, k and components v = (v1, v2, v3) = v1 i + v2 j + v3 k.
Add and subtract vectors, and use the zero vector 0 and −v, algebraically and geometrically.
Multiply by a scalar kv and recognise parallel vectors.
Find the magnitude |v| and unit vectors v/|v|.
Use OA = a, OB = b and the displacement AB = b − a; the distance between A and B is the magnitude of AB.
Prove geometrical properties using vectors.
Define the scalar product and use its properties: v·w = w·v, u·(v + w) = u·v + u·w, (kv)·w = k(v·w), v·v = |v|^2.
Find the angle between vectors from v·w = |v||w| cosθ.
For non-zero vectors, v·w = 0 means perpendicular; for parallel vectors |v·w| = |v||w|.
Write the vector equation of a line, r = a + λb, in 2D and 3D, with a a position and b a direction.
Know parametric form x = x0 + λl, y = y0 + λm, z = z0 + λn and Cartesian form (x − x0)/l = (y − y0)/m = (z − z0)/n.
Find the angle between two lines using the scalar product of their direction vectors.
Apply to simple kinematics, with λ as time, b as velocity and |b| as speed.
Tell coincident, parallel, intersecting and skew lines apart; skew lines are non-parallel and never meet in 3D.
Find points of intersection.
Define the vector (cross) product v × w = |v||w| sinθ n, with n a unit normal fixed by the right-hand screw rule.
Use its properties: v × w = −w × v, u × (v + w) = u × v + u × w, (kv) × w = k(v × w), v × v = 0.
For non-zero vectors, v × w = 0 means parallel.
Interpret |v × w| geometrically, using it for the area of a parallelogram and a triangle.

booklet.label: Area of a parallelogram from vectors

bullets.text: Write a plane as r = a + λb + μc, with b and c non-parallel vectors in the plane.
Write a plane as r · n = a · n, with n a normal and a a point on the plane.
Write the Cartesian equation ax + by + cz = d.

items.name: Intersections and angles of lines and planes

bullets.text: Solve for where a line meets a plane, where two planes meet and where three planes meet, and interpret each solution geometrically.
Find the angle between a line and a plane, and between two planes.
Link to systems of linear equations (1.16).
Use the terms population, sample, random sample, discrete data and continuous data.
Judge how reliable a data source is and where sampling bias arises, including missing data and recording errors.
Interpret outliers: a value more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the nearest quartile; some are valid sample members, some are errors.
Know sampling techniques and their effectiveness: simple random, convenience, systematic, quota, stratified.
Present discrete and continuous data in frequency tables (class intervals as inequalities without gaps).
Draw histograms: frequency histograms with equal class intervals; frequency density histograms are not required.
Use cumulative frequency graphs to find median, quartiles, percentiles, range and IQR.
Draw and read box and whisker diagrams, with outliers marked by crosses; compare two distributions and judge from symmetry whether data may be normal.
Find mean, median and mode; find the mean both by formula and with technology.
Estimate the mean of grouped data from mid-interval values; find the modal class (equal class intervals only).
Find IQR, standard deviation and variance; standard deviation and variance of a sample use technology only, and squaring the standard deviation gives the variance.
Say how adding to or scaling all data values changes mean and standard deviation (e.g. subtract 3, or double all values).
Find quartiles of discrete data using technology, knowing that methods differ so by-hand and technology values may differ.
Describe linear correlation of bivariate data: positive, zero, negative; strong, weak, none.
Find Pearson's r with technology (hand calculation optional); critical values are given; r is only meaningful for linear relationships.
Draw scatter diagrams and lines of best fit by eye through the mean point.
Separate correlation from causation: correlation does not imply causation.
Find the regression line of y on x with technology, and use it for prediction.
Interpret the parameters a and b in y = ax + b.
Know the dangers of extrapolation, and that a y on x line cannot reliably predict x from y.
Use the vocabulary of probability: trial, outcome, equally likely, relative frequency, sample space (U), event; list sample spaces or tabulate them.
Find P(A) = n(A)/n(U), and tell experimental (relative frequency) from theoretical probability.
Use complementary events A and A′.
Find the expected number of occurrences, e.g. 128 students, P(absent) = 0.1, expect 12.8.
Find probabilities from Venn, tree and sample-space diagrams or outcome tables, with or without replacement.
Use P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), including the non-exclusive meaning of 'or'.
Use mutually exclusive events: P(A ∩ B) = 0.
Use conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) and P(A ∩ B) = P(B)P(A|B).
Use independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
Problems can be solved from diagrams without explicit formulae.

items.name: Discrete random variables and expected value

bullets.text: Work with discrete random variables and probability distributions given as a table or a formula such as P(X = x) = (1/18)(4 + x) for x in {1, 2, 3}.
Find the expected value E(X) of a discrete random variable.
Apply to problems; E(X) = 0 means a fair game where X is a player's gain.
Recognise situations modelled by a binomial distribution and find binomial probabilities with technology.
Use the mean and variance of a binomial distribution; the formal proof is not required.
Link to expected number of occurrences (SL 4.5).
Know the normal distribution and curve, its properties and diagrams, and its natural occurrence.
Know about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of data within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.
Find normal probabilities with technology.
Find inverse normal values with technology when mean and standard deviation are given; no standardising to z is involved.
Find the regression line of x on y and use it for prediction.
Know that an x on y line cannot reliably predict y from x.
Use P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) for conditional probability, formally defined, and P(A ∩ B) = P(B)P(A|B).
Use P(A|B) = P(A) = P(A|B′) for independent events, and test for independence.
Standardise normal variables to z-values; z counts standard deviations from the mean.
Do inverse normal calculations when the mean or standard deviation is unknown, using technology and z-values.
Use Bayes' theorem for up to three events.
Link to independent events (SL 4.6).
Find the variance of a discrete random variable; use E(X), E(X^2) and Var(X) = E(X^2) − [E(X)]^2.
Work with a continuous random variable through its density function f, where the total integral of f(x) is 1, including piecewise densities.
Find the mode (maximum of the density) and the median m, from ∫ f(x)dx = 1/2 up to m.
Find mean, variance and standard deviation of discrete and continuous random variables; use E(X) for fair games.
Apply linear transformations: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X).

booklet.label: Standard deviation from a frequency table
Linear transformation of a random variable

items.name: Limits and derivative as rate of change

bullets.text: Meet the idea of a limit, estimating limit values from a table or graph; formal analytic methods of finding limits are not required.
Treat the derivative both as the slope function and as a rate of change; write it as dy/dx, f′(x), dV/dr or ds/dt.
Understand the gradient of a curve informally as a limit.
Identify increasing and decreasing functions and the intervals where they occur.
Interpret f′(x) > 0, f′(x) = 0 and f′(x) < 0 graphically.
Differentiate f(x) = ax^n to get anx^(n−1), for n an integer.
Differentiate sums of such terms, e.g. ax^n + bx^(n−1) + …, where all exponents are integers.
Get the equation of the tangent and of the normal at a chosen point, analytically and with technology.
Integrate ax^n + bx^(n−1) + … as anti-differentiation, for integer n ≠ −1.
Use a boundary condition to find the constant, e.g. dy/dx = 3x^2 + x with y = 10 at x = 1.
Evaluate definite integrals with technology.
Find the area between a curve y = f(x) > 0 and the x-axis; link anti-derivatives, definite integrals and area, and write a correct integral expression first.
Differentiate x^n (n rational), sinx, cosx, e^x and lnx.
Differentiate sums and multiples of these functions.
Use the chain rule for composite functions, e.g. e^(x^2 + 2) and sin(3x − 1).
Use the product and quotient rules.
Find the second derivative, using notation d^2y/dx^2 and f″(x).
Describe graph behaviour and the relationship between the graphs of f, f′ and f″, using technology to explore.
Find local maximum and minimum points.
Test them by the sign change of f′ or the sign of f″ (f″ > 0 minimum, f″ < 0 maximum).
Solve optimisation problems such as profit, area and volume.
Find points of inflexion, with zero or non-zero gradient: f″ = 0 and changes sign; f″ = 0 alone is not sufficient (e.g. y = x^4 at the origin).
Describe concavity as concave-up (f″ > 0) or concave-down (f″ < 0).
Solve kinematics problems with displacement s, velocity v, acceleration a and total distance: v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt = d^2s/dt^2.
Find displacement from t1 to t2 as ∫ v(t) dt.
Find distance travelled as ∫ |v(t)| dt.
Know that speed is the magnitude of velocity.
Integrate x^n (n rational), sinx, cosx, 1/x (∫ (1/x)dx = ln|x| + C) and e^x.
Integrate composites of these with a linear function ax + b, e.g. cos(2x + 3) gives (1/2)sin(2x + 3) + C.
Integrate by inspection (reverse chain rule) or substitution for ∫ k g′(x) f(g(x)) dx, e.g. ∫2x(x^2 + 1)^4 dx, ∫4x sin x^2 dx, ∫ sinx/cosx dx.
Evaluate definite integrals analytically, using ∫ g′(x)dx from a to b = g(b) − g(a); some can only be found with technology.
Find the area between a curve y = f(x) and the x-axis when f is positive or negative, without technology, writing a correct integral expression first.
Find areas between curves; technology can show how integrals relate to areas.

booklet.label: Area between a curve and the x-axis

bullets.text: Understand continuity and differentiability at a point informally; examinations do not ask you to test them.
Understand limits (convergence and divergence), linking to infinite geometric sequences.
Use the first-principles definition f′(x) = lim (f(x + h) − f(x))/h as h → 0, for polynomials only.
Find higher derivatives, using notation d^n y/dx^n and f^(n)(x).
Evaluate limits of f(x)/g(x) as x → a and as x → ∞ using l'Hôpital's rule or the Maclaurin series, for the forms 0/0 and ∞/∞, e.g. lim sinθ/θ = 1.
Use l'Hôpital's rule repeatedly.

items.name: Implicit differentiation, related rates and optimization

bullets.text: Differentiate implicitly.
Solve related rates of change problems.
Solve optimisation problems using the chain rule or implicit differentiation, including optimum at an end point.
Differentiate the trig functions tan x, cot x, sec x and cosec x, the general exponential a^x and logarithm log_a x, and the inverse trig functions arcsin x, arccos x and arctan x.

Integrate the derivatives of these functions, and composites with a linear function, e.g. 1/(x^2 + 2x + 5) gives (1/2)arctan((x + 1)/2) + C and sec^2(2x + 5) gives (1/2)tan(2x + 5) + C; an indefinite integral is a family of curves.
Use partial fractions to rearrange an integrand, e.g. 1/(x^2 + 3x + 2) gives ln|(x + 1)/(x + 2)| + C.
Integrate by substitution; substitutions are given in exams when the integral is not of the form ∫ k g′(x) f(g(x)) dx.
Integrate by parts, e.g. ∫x sinx dx, ∫lnx dx, ∫arcsinx dx.
Use integration by parts repeatedly, e.g. ∫x^2 e^x dx and ∫e^x sinx dx.
Find the area between a curve and the y-axis over a given interval.
Find the volume when a region is rotated around either axis.

booklet.label: Area between a curve and the y-axis

bullets.text: Solve first-order differential equations.
Solve dy/dx = f(x, y) numerically with Euler's method, using the step x_{n+1} = x_n + h for constant h.
Solve by separating variables, e.g. the logistic equation dn/dt = kn(a − n), using partial fractions.
Solve homogeneous equations dy/dx = f(y/x) using the substitution y = vx.
Solve y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) with the integrating factor.
Use Maclaurin series to get expansions of e^x, sinx, cosx, arctanx, ln(1 + x) and (1 + x)^p for p rational.
Get other series by substitution, products, integration and differentiation, e.g. replace x with x^2 for e^(x^2), or expand e^x sinx.
Develop Maclaurin series from differential equations.
